description: AstroByte is a team from Veracruz, Mexico, led by a fullstack developer with AI/ML and data experience. We want to process SAR imagery, detect changes over time and show them in an interactive web map. Looking for teammates in remote sensing, data analysis, ML, data viz and design/storytelling. Beginners welcome. We speak Spanish and English.
summary: Water's Dance is an open-source, bilingual (Spanish/English) interactive story map and explorer built on ten real NISAR L-band passes over the Veracruz–Boca del Río metropolitan area, Mexico, during the 2026 rainy season (June 25 – October 23). It turns radar backscatter into things a resident or a city planner can read: where open water appears and disappears, how soil moisture rises after rain, why the city's protected interdune lagoons look like vegetation to the radar, and why a 12-day revisit cannot catch an urban flood that drains in hours. It connects those observations to our stochastic flood forecast, where soil moisture is the initial condition that decides whether 60 mm of rain soaks in or runs into the street.
details:
Live story map: https://darw1ng.github.io/El-Ojo-de-tlaloc/

Open-source code (MIT license): https://github.com/Darw1ng/El-Ojo-de-tlaloc

What it does

A scroll-driven story in twelve chapters, followed by a free explorer. The explorer has nine layers (HH·HV composite, HH, HV, open water, change against the season median, soil-moisture index, water permanence, lagoons by radar signature, and a 3D hexagon grid). It also has a time slider over the ten passes with daily rainfall, a before/after swipe between any two dates, and a click-anywhere popup with that pixel's HH/HV time series.

How it works

  1. scripts/nisar_gcov.py searches the ASF catalog and reads only the metropolitan window (2,148 × 2,365 pixels at 10 m) from each remote 4.8 GB GCOV HDF5 file with earthaccess. Ten dates take about eight minutes instead of a 47 GB download.
  2. scripts/nisar_productos.py applies a Lee speckle filter and a relative radiometric normalization against stable urban targets. The provisional products drifted about 1 dB between dates, and the city revealed it. It then thresholds open water at the histogram valley (HH < −14.8 dB, HV < −19.8 dB), masks the sea, beach and runways, and computes per-pixel change and a change-detection soil-moisture index. Finally it crosses everything with NASA POWER rainfall and with OpenStreetMap lagoons, schools, clinics and emergency services, on the project's hexagonal grid.
  3. The web app (frontend/nisar/) is plain HTML/CSS/JS with Mapbox GL JS (it falls back to MapLibre GL JS over OpenStreetMap if Mapbox is unavailable). It needs no build step and runs as a static site.

What we found

  • Inland open water ranged from 1.1 to 2.2 km² per pass. Most of the change is at the northern end of the Mandinga lagoon system, between 1.0 and 1.45 km².
  • The soil-moisture index went from 0.39 (August 12) to 0.59 (September 17). It tracks the previous three days of rain moderately (r = 0.36).
  • None of the 58 mapped lagoons shows an open-water signature: 29 look like vegetation over water and 29 are mixed. Tarimoya lagoon brightened 2.3 dB from June to late September, consistent with water rising under vegetation. This is a hypothesis to check in the field.
  • No school, clinic or emergency service was within 200 m of temporary open water on any pass. Urban floods are faster than the revisit, which is exactly why radar soil moisture belongs inside a forecast.

Limits we state openly

The products are provisional, so the normalization also removes any scene-wide signal. Rainfall comes from a single half-degree NASA POWER point. The moisture index is relative, not volumetric. The lagoon interpretation has not been checked in the field.

Tools

Python (numpy, scipy, scikit-image, h5py, rasterio, earthaccess, Pillow), FastAPI for the forecasting backend, Mapbox GL JS, MapLibre GL JS, Leaflet, HyperFrames for the demo video, ffmpeg.

Use of AI

We used Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code) as a coding and writing assistant to write the download and processing scripts, build the web app, draft the bilingual story text and this summary, and assemble the demo video. Every number in the story is computed from the NISAR, NASA POWER and OpenStreetMap data by the scripts in the repository. No imagery, map or data value was generated by AI. The team reviewed the method, the results and the stated limits.
